name: Massimiliano Allegri
scopeNote: Three counted spells: AC Milan 2010-06-25 to 2014-01-13; Juventus 2014-07-16 to 2019-05-26; Juventus 2021-07-01 to 2024-05-17. Style is described by tactical sources as pragmatic, formation-flexible (4-3-3/4-3-1-2 at Milan; 3-5-2, 4-3-1-2, 4-2-3-1, 4-4-2 and later 3-5-2/5-3-2 at Juventus) with a compact, passive 4-4-2 or 5-3-2 block, wide build-up and counters; 'corto muso' is a media/club label (Agnelli 2021) that Allegri himself pushed back on, not a tactical system. Marking: Hudl describes ball-oriented marking with man-marking of free players in pressing (zonal block, man-oriented pressing), no source calls it pure zonal or man-to-man. Coverage of the Milan spell is thin and mostly tier C. Excluded-spell dates are approximate and unresearched. Dated Milan departure and Juventus dates come from the user's decision, not re-verified here.
openQuestions: Agnelli (2021-07-27, ecoseven/Adnkronos) attributes the 'corto muso' theory to Allegri; no primary first appearance of Allegri's own phrase found. Allegri later (Spezia press conference, 2022) said it referred to the league race, per a search summary only (unverified).
'Il calcio non è matematica': the SOS Fanta page (2024-02-16) returned no readable paragraph, so the quote is not verified in this file.
No tier A-B source found for Allegri's Milan 2010-14 tactics or set-piece routines; SoccerTutor and Coaches' Voice mostly cover the first Juventus spell.

Marking: sources describe man-oriented duties inside a zonal-looking block (Hudl: 'mark all opponents around' the ball); Muntari shadowing Xavi (Milan v Barcelona 2012) is a single-match man-marking assignment.
SoccerTutor article covers mainly Conte's 2013-14 3-5-2; only the 4-2-3-1 paragraph is used as Allegri evidence.

sources.title: Massimiliano Allegri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: Prioritising a 3-5-2 built on the revered back three of Andrea Barzagli, Leonardo Bonucci and Giorgio Chiellini, Juve's attacking width was provided by their wing-backs; of their three central midfielders, one remained withdrawn to defend, and the other two advanced through the inside channels and alongside their wing-backs to support their front two.

sources.title: Massimiliano Allegri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: Juve's attacking width was provided by their wing-backs; of their three central midfielders, one remained withdrawn to defend, and the other two advanced through the inside channels and alongside their wing-backs to support their front two.

sources.title: Massimiliano Allegri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: A further change involved Allegri reorganising his team into a 4-2-3-1 (below) built on the double pivot of Khedira and Miralem Pjanic, and led by Gonzalo Higuaín, following his arrival from Napoli, ensuring Dybala instead featured as their number 10 and Mandzukic towards the left

sources.title: Massimiliano Allegri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: That Mandzukic was instructed to so often attack infield meant that Alex Sandro was responsible for providing their width from left-back, and that their double pivot was responsible for providing defensive cover through the inside channel and therefore made fewer forward runs.

sources.title: Massimiliano Allegri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: Allegri's willingness to adapt to the players at his disposal meant him also increasingly using a 4-4-2 or 4-3-3 – sometimes, mid-match – across the final two seasons of that first spell as Juve's manager, as was demanded by their opponents' shape.

sources.title: Massimiliano Allegri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: Cristiano Ronaldo's arrival, and Bonucci's return from AC Milan and with it his distribution, meant Ronaldo replacing Mandzukic and a reduced emphasis on Pjanic to build play from the defensive half.

sources.title: Massimiliano Allegri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: Allegri has long favoured an organised defence and a disciplined, somewhat reserved, defensive block, but there remain occasions when he oversees a high press. When Juve's back three was being implemented, their wing-backs withdrew into defence to form a back five (below) that was protected by three central midfielders prioritising the spaces in front of their three central defenders.

sources.title: Massimiliano Allegri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: Their front two worked to cover the central spaces and to force possession wide; one also operated from a slightly withdrawn position to offer cover against their opposing defensive midfielder, a tactic that proved particularly influential against opponents largely reliant on that midfielder to dictate play.

sources.title: Massimiliano Allegri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: The presence of a back five also meant that the most central defender – most regularly Bonucci – could react aggressively when opponents advanced beyond Juve's midfield, potentially to press, in the knowledge that a back four would remain in place behind him

sources.title: Massimiliano Allegri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: When their shape evolved to instead feature a back four, if not a 4-2-3-1, their most common defensive shape was a 4-4-2 that was favoured when they were defending for lengthier periods, and not when applying a high press. Mandzukic and Cuadrado withdrew into midfield to provide cover from alongside Pjanic and Khedira and in front of the full-backs who had retreated into defence.

sources.title: Massimiliano Allegri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: It was while in that 4-4-1-1 that Juve's two central midfielders withdrew into deeper positions than those adopted in their 4-4-2, and pressed with reduced aggression, ultimately prioritising defending the spaces between the lines because of the reduced number of defenders behind them.

sources.title: Massimiliano Allegri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: By Bonucci or another advancing, there were also times attacks were delayed long enough for their three midfielders to press from behind or to the side of the ball, and potentially to force it wide, to where their wing-backs were proven at defending one-on-one.

sources.title: Massimiliano Allegri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: When their defensive block was established, Juve were content to frustrate opponents and to defend for lengthy periods of organised defending.

sources.title: Massimiliano Allegri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice

sources.title: Allegri's Juventus: Champions Once More? (Tifo Football, transcript)
sources.evidence: Allegri is tactically flexible and adapts his formations to the players available. While he has used a 3-5-2, Juventus has more recently often lined up in a 4-2-3-1, which can fluctuate to a 4-4-2 when defending.

sources.title: Allegri's Juventus: Champions Once More? (Tifo Football, transcript)
sources.evidence: When Juventus loses possession, they tend to drop into a more defensive 4-4-2 configuration. They are more passive in their approach, preferring to compress space and wait for opposition mistakes rather than aggressively pressing.

sources.title: Allegri's Juventus: Champions Once More? (Tifo Football, transcript)
sources.evidence: Allegri likes his team to drop into a more defensive 4-4-2 configuration with the wide midfielders dropping in alongside the two central midfielders in the double pivot however given the fact that both P an itch and Khedira are played for their ball playing prowess rather than their explicitly defensive capabilities the Aventis forward players will often press the opposition defenders aggressively at first to allow the central midfielders to adjust to a defensive position

sources.title: Allegri's Juventus: Champions Once More? (Tifo Football, transcript)

sources.title: Juventus Tactics: Conte, Allegri and the 3-5-2 Dynasty (SoccerTutor)
sources.evidence: Allegri's 4-2-3-1 had a distinctive attacking pattern. He asked the forward (9) and both wingers (11 and 7) to drop between the lines, creating a constant dilemma for defenders. If the defender didn't follow, the Juventus player turned with space. If the defender did follow, that movement opened the channel behind for a runner.

sources.title: Juventus Tactics: Conte, Allegri and the 3-5-2 Dynasty (SoccerTutor)
sources.evidence: Miralem Pjanic was central to making it work. His vision and passing range let him read each scenario and pick the right ball: a straight pass through the middle for the number 10's diagonal run, a diagonal between centre-back and full-back for the left winger, or an aerial pass to the right winger when that flank opened up.

sources.title: How Defensive Effort Is Powering Juventus' Challenge for the Serie A Title (Hudl)
sources.evidence: Allegri's ideal 5-3-2 should be the one seen in the game against Napoli: in front of Szczęsny played the defensive trio made up of Gatti on the right, Bremer in the center and Danilo on the left. On the wings, Kostic to the left and Cambiaso to the right

sources.title: How Defensive Effort Is Powering Juventus' Challenge for the Serie A Title (Hudl)
sources.evidence: high pressure is not constant but rather used in particular situations: goal kicks from the goalkeeper and backside passes towards the defense. Juventus use the ball as the first reference, to then mark all opponents around it. The pressing style changes according to the opponent's position.

sources.title: How Defensive Effort Is Powering Juventus' Challenge for the Serie A Title (Hudl)
sources.evidence: Against a three-man defense like Inter's, one of the inside forwards joins the two strikers to pressure the center-backs, making sure there's a 3v3 situation when the opponents build up from the back. When this happens, Juve's center-back on that side moves forward to mark the man who is left free by the Mezzala's movement

sources.title: How Defensive Effort Is Powering Juventus' Challenge for the Serie A Title (Hudl)
sources.evidence: the best move of Allegri's football remains the positional defense in their own half. Juve compacts vertically in their 5-3-2 that wants to close off the center of the pitch for the opponents, forcing them towards the wings. There, with the help of the sideline, the inside forward and winger pressure more aggressively on the opponents. Juventus' PPDA data – 12.04, the seventh-highest in the league

sources.title: How Defensive Effort Is Powering Juventus' Challenge for the Serie A Title (Hudl)
sources.evidence: Juventus don't have a very elaborate first phase of possession to avoid losing dangerous balls to the opponents. When advancing in the build-up, they prefer not to seek passes in central areas, which would make it easier for their opponents to win the ball back and counterattack quickly. This is why Allegri mostly asks his players to develop the buildup in wide areas, with lots of switch of plays

sources.title: How Defensive Effort Is Powering Juventus' Challenge for the Serie A Title (Hudl)
sources.evidence: Juventus sometimes do the opposite: they defend with three center-backs but build up with a four-man defense, with Kostic lying deep as a left full-back and Gatti going wide as the right full-back.
